title: Pressure-cooker bone broth
subtitle: Slow-food depth in fast time
excerpt: A deep, gelatinous broth made from oxtail and vegetables under pressure. Ready in 2 hours instead of overnight, with the same rich, collagen-dense result.
sourceNotes: Long-simmered bone broths appear in kitchen traditions worldwide; the modern revival draws on traditional stock-making covered in Fergus Henderson's Nose to Tail Eating (1999) and Sally Fallon's Nourishing Traditions (1999). The pressure-cooker method achieves similar gelatin extraction in 2 hours.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in 250 ml or 500 ml portions for up to 6 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily, most 6-litre pressure cookers will take 1.6 kg of oxtail. The broth freezes well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days. The fat cap on top acts as a seal, remove it just before using.

content.text: Bone broth is a long-cooked stock made primarily for sipping or as a base for soups, made from oxtail and aromatics. The pressure cooker cuts the usual 12-hour simmering down to 2 hours, producing a broth that sets firmly in the fridge, a sign that the gelatin has fully dissolved from the bone and joint material.

The acidity of the cider vinegar helps draw minerals from the bones; add it to the water before you start. Unlike a clearer stock, this broth is not filtered as finely, a slight cloudiness is expected and does not affect the flavour or texture.
Drink it warm in a mug or use it as the base for soups and braises. The fat that sets on top when cold lifts off cleanly and can be used for cooking.

Put the oxtail, carrot, celery, onion, garlic, cider vinegar, bay leaves, and thyme into the pressure cooker. Add enough cold water to cover by 3 cm, approximately 1.8 litres. Season with a teaspoon of salt. Seal the lid.
Bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 2 hours. The longer time extracts more gelatin than a shorter stock cook.

Allow the pressure to release naturally, at least 20 minutes, or until the float valve drops. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin-lined sieve into a large bowl. Discard the solids. Cool the broth quickly in a sink of cold water, then refrigerate.

Once cold, lift off the fat layer. Taste the broth and add salt as needed. The broth should be a dark amber and slightly viscous when warm. If it has set to a firm jelly when cold, the gelatin extraction was successful.

rows.symptom: The broth did not set to a jelly
rows.cause: The oxtail pieces had insufficient joint material, or the cooking time was too short.
rows.fix: The broth will still taste good. For a firmer set next time, cook for an additional 30 minutes and source oxtail with large tail sections rather than the thin tip pieces.

rows.cause: Too much cider vinegar was used, or it was added after cooking rather than at the start.
rows.fix: The acidity should cook out during the 2-hour pressure cook. If the finished broth still tastes sharp, dilute with a little hot water and season with extra salt.

rows.cause: A quick pressure release disturbs the proteins, making the liquid cloudy.
rows.fix: Always use a natural pressure release for stocks. Cloudiness does not affect flavour; for a clearer result, strain through a muslin cloth or a coffee filter.

rows.symptom: The oxtail still looks undercooked after straining
rows.cause: The oxtail pieces were too large for the pressure to penetrate fully, or the cooker did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Return the strained oxtail and 300 ml of the broth to the pressure cooker and cook for an additional 30 minutes. The meat from oxtail cooked for stock, while not pretty, makes excellent rillettes or a filling for pies.

content.text: Freeze in 250 ml portions in zip-lock bags or rigid containers for up to 6 months. Reheat from frozen by placing the sealed container in a bowl of warm water or by transferring to a saucepan over low heat.

The revival of bone broth in home kitchens is partly nostalgia and partly practicality, it is what frugal cooks have always made from cuts that simmer rather than roast. The pressure cooker makes the method achievable without a whole day's commitment. Warm, seasoned, and drunk from a mug, it is one of those kitchen preparations that falls squarely between cooking and making a pot of tea.
